title: Ang 94: Majh begins
hook: Guru Ram Das opens the raga
tomorrow: what do you write when you miss someone that much?

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bhagats close it. Kabir, Trilochan, Beni and Ravidas had the last word in Sri Rag. Turn the page to a new raga.

Ask a group chat who they'd give anything to meet and the answers pour in: a singer, a player, a grandparent who's gone. On ang 94, Majh, the Granth's second raga, opens with Guru Ram Das's answer. It isn't a famous name. It's whoever would introduce him to his Beloved.
screen: `WHO WOULD YOU GIVE ANYTHING TO MEET?` → `MAJH, THE SECOND RAGA.` → `WHOEVER LEADS TO THE BELOVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the question underneath: can a friend lead you to God? Guru Ram Das's first Majh hymn longs for exactly that. In paraphrase: if some friend, some saint, would come and bring me to meet my Beloved, I would give myself to them. The longing is for the One. But the road runs through a person. That's the Sikh picture of sangat, the holy company: the people who make the Name easier to remember, just by being around. Now a neighbor who says something close, in its own words. In the Buddhist scriptures, the Upaddha Sutta, the Buddha's attendant Ananda says that good friendship must be half of the holy life. The Buddha answers, in paraphrase: don't say that, Ananda. Good friendship is the whole of the holy life. And the Buddha calls himself that kind of friend to everyone who walks the path. So two traditions agree that nobody walks this alone; the friend is not a bonus, the friend is the road. And here's the honest difference. In the sutta, the good friend leads along the noble path, toward freedom from suffering, with no Beloved Lord waiting at the end. In Majh, the friend's whole job is to bring you to the Beloved, the One the Guru aches to meet. Same road, a different meeting at the end of it.
screen: `CAN A FRIEND LEAD YOU TO GOD?` · `MAJH: BRING ME TO MY BELOVED.` · `UPADDHA: FRIENDSHIP IS THE WHOLE.` · `SAME ROAD, A DIFFERENT MEETING.` · then, large: `MAJH BEGINS.`

segments.voice: If a Gurbani app is open, read the first hymn on ang 94 before you begin. Count, slowly, on your fingers, the people who have made it easier for you to be good, or to remember what matters: a teacher, a grandparent, a friend who drove you somewhere when you needed it. For each finger, picture a face. Then rest your hands in your lap and let the sit be gratitude without words.
Ang 94. The page where Majh begins, with Guru Ram Das longing for the friend who leads to the Beloved.
On the way out: majh begins, and it begins with a friend, because nobody walks this road alone. Rest well.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of the sangat, the holy company at the gurdwara and beyond, as the place where the Name is easier to remember; Majh hymns are sung in kirtan, and readers in order reach them after Sri Rag.

fork.reveal: Guru Ram Das would give himself to the friend who leads to the Beloved; the Buddha calls good friendship the whole of the holy life. they differ on where the road ends, not on needing company.

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 written: shape wisdom, with the weekly unity thread. Question: can a friend lead you to God? Sikh answer from Majh (ang 94) and the sangat; neighbor: Buddhism, in its own source (Samyutta Nikaya 45.2, Upaddha Sutta). One shared thing (nobody walks it alone) and one honest difference (the Buddhist path's goal is freedom from suffering, with no Beloved Lord; Majh's friend leads to the Beloved). No ranking, no 'all the same'.

Ang 94 line: paraphrase of Majh Mahala 4 (koee aan milaavai meraa preetam piaaraa hau tis peh aap vechaaee, or the nearby koee sajan sant milai vadbhaagee line). Confirm the exact line and that it is on ang 94 in the opening hymn.

Upaddha Sutta: Ananda says admirable friendship is half the holy life; the Buddha says it is the whole, and that beings are freed by relying on him as their good friend. Paraphrased (no public-domain translation quoted). A Buddhist reviewer should confirm the summary and the 'no Beloved Lord' framing of the difference.
'Majh, the Granth's second raga': follows the outline (Sri Rag, then Majh). Confirm.
